chief_complaint: painless, soft, mobile subcutaneous lump on back
hpi_details: A 74-year-old female presents to the clinic with a painless, soft, mobile subcutaneous lump on her back. She first noticed it several months ago, and it has been slowly enlarging without pain or other associated symptoms.
ideas: She thinks the lump is just an accumulation of harmless fatty tissue or a blocked sebaceous cyst under her skin.
concerns: She is worried that the lump might actually be a slow-growing malignant sarcoma that could invade her spine if ignored.
expectations: She hopes to get an ultrasound or biopsy today to confirm it is not cancerous and find out if it needs removal.

Standard management for Dorsal Lipoma emphasizes reassurance, with elective surgical excision if bothersome or large, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

teaching.one_liner: A benign, slow-growing tumor of fat cells presenting as a soft, mobile, painless lump beneath the skin.
differentials: Soft tissue sarcoma (if rapidly growing or fixed)
red_flags: Rapid growth, hardness, or fixation to underlying tissue — reconsider sarcoma

must_ask.say: Is the lump soft and does it move easily under your skin?
How long have you had it, and has it grown quickly or slowly?
Do you have similar lumps anywhere else on your body?
What's making you want to have it looked at now?

history.answer: I noticed a soft bump on my upper back a few months ago, and I wanted to have it checked out.
I first felt it about four months ago while reaching back in the shower.
It is right on my upper back, between my shoulder blades and slightly to the right side.
It has grown very slowly over the past few months, starting like a small grape and now feeling like a golf ball.
It is about the size of a golf ball, and there is only that one lump.
It feels squishy and soft, and when I nudge it with my fingers, it slides around easily under the skin.
No, it does not hurt at all, even when I press directly on it or lean against a chair.
No, the skin over it looks completely normal, and I have not seen any new or changing moles anywhere.
No, it has never bled, broken open, or formed any scabs.
No, there is no redness, warmth, or any fluid coming from it.
No, there is no little hole or dark spot in the middle, and nothing ever squeezes out of it.
No, it stays the same size all the time and does not change when I move or exercise.
No, I have never had an injury, cut, or surgery on that part of my back.
history.topic: Previous trauma or surgery at site

history.answer: No, I have had no fever, night sweats, or unexpected weight loss, and no swollen glands anywhere.
I have never spent much time baking in the sun, and I have never had a severe blistering sunburn.
No, neither I nor anyone in my family has ever had skin cancer or melanoma.
No, I do not have diabetes, and I have never taken steroids or immune-suppressing drugs.
No, I have left it alone and have not tried to pop, squeeze, or treat it at home.
I thought it was probably just a harmless little pocket of fat or a clogged cyst that slowly formed under my skin.
I'm worried that this lump might actually be a malignant tumor that could grow deep into my spine if we leave it alone.
I'm hoping you can arrange an ultrasound to prove it's completely benign and let me know if it has to be removed.
My medical history is unremarkable, and I do not have any chronic conditions.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital stays.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter pills, or supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only have an occasional small glass of wine on special occasions.
I am retired and live comfortably at home with my husband.
There is no history of cancer, tumors, or major inherited conditions in my family.

exam.finding: Well-nourished, comfortable-appearing elderly female in no acute distress.
Blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.6°C, SpO2 98% on room air.
A soft, mobile, non-tender, lobulated subcutaneous mass measuring approximately 4 cm on the upper back, with normal overlying skin and no punctum, redness, or induration.
Palpation of the upper thoracic back confirms a soft, well-circumscribed mass easily moved over deep tissues without fixation to underlying muscle.
No cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy palpable.
Normal thoracic spinal alignment with no midline spinous process tenderness or paraspinal muscle spasm.
